cards.explanation: The answer is letters and a gift. Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, because he had heard about Hezekiah's illness and recovery (Isaiah 39:1). Letters and a gift, and all of it because of news that a man had gotten well. I think that's a pretty warm way to say hello, friends.

The answer is False. It was not a few treasures. Hezekiah showed the envoys the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil and his entire armory (Isaiah 39:2). The text says there was "…nothing in his palace or in all his dominion…" that he did not show them. When I show somebody my bakery, friends, I at least keep one cookie jar closed.

The answer is carried off to Babylon. Isaiah says the LORD declares that everything in King Hezekiah's palace, and all that his fathers had stored up until that day, "…will be carried off to Babylon." Then comes the line, "Nothing will be left, says the LORD." (Isaiah 39:6) The envoys who had just gotten the grand tour of that palace were from Babylon, the very place it would go, friends.

The answer is descendants. Isaiah brings the LORD's word to King Hezekiah: "…some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon." (Isaiah 39:7) Friends, this part is heavy. It's not only about treasure and things. It reaches Hezekiah's own family line.

The answer is that it is good. Isaiah had just told King Hezekiah that everything in his palace would be carried off to Babylon, and that some of his descendants would be taken away. Hezekiah answered Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." (Isaiah 39:8) Friends, that's a surprising thing to say after hearing all of that.

The answer is that at least his own lifetime will have peace. The text says Hezekiah thought, "At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime." (Isaiah 39:8) That's his own thought, friends, and it's right there in the verse. I think it's a quiet, sad note to end on.
